segments.caption: Day 3 of 100 Days of Machine Learning: your first ML project, the real way.
8 steps, and the real problems data scientists face at every one. Save this one!
Courses give you clean data and a happy ending. Real projects don't.
Let's follow one real project, predicting flat prices in Bangalore, and see what actually goes wrong.
Step 1, problem definition. Your manager says: predict flat prices. That's it.
The real problem: a vague ask. Prices for whom? Buyers, sellers, or a bank? And how accurate is good enough?
So you ask questions first, and agree on success: say, within 8 lakh.
Step 2, data collection. The data you need is never in one place.
Listings sit on different websites. Half have no price. And most are asking prices, not what flats actually sold for.
So you combine sources, and note what each one really measures.
Step 3, data cleaning. This is where most of your time goes.
"2 BHK", "2bhk" and "two bedroom", all meaning the same thing. Area in sq ft and sq m. And the same flat, posted by 3 different brokers.
You standardise everything, remove duplicates, and flag anything suspicious.
Step 4, exploratory data analysis. You plot everything, and find surprises.
Prices near one new metro station jumped 30% in a year. Is that real, or a data error?
So you check with people who know the market before trusting a pattern.
Step 5, the train-test split. The trap: mixing old and new sales together.
Prices keep rising, so you test on the most recent months, exactly how the model will be used.
Step 6, model training. The model scores amazingly well. Too well.
It was using days on market, which you only know after the flat sells. That's called data leakage. Remove it, and you get an honest score.
Step 7, model evaluation. The average error looks fine.
But for luxury villas and brand new areas, it's way off. So you check accuracy group by group, not just the overall number.
Step 8, deployment. The model goes live. 6 months later, interest rates change, and predictions slowly go wrong.
That's model drift. So you monitor it, and retrain regularly.
So here's the real checklist.
Ask before you build. Know your sources. Clean everything. Question every pattern. Test on recent data. Watch for leakage. Check every group. Monitor after launch.
Save this. This is what the job really looks like.
Your turn: what takes most of a data scientist's time? Vote in the caption poll!
